Draw any of the three views with bundled records. Each opening lesson includes its own setup. Continue online for data import, advanced workflows and complete research examples.


## Download and install {#installation}

### Download and install {#installation-requirements}

Use R ≥ 4.1.0 and ggplot2 ≥ 4.0.0. Run these commands in R. CRAN supplies ggchord and its required dependencies.

```{r example-1, eval=FALSE}
install.packages("ggchord")
library(ggchord)
packageVersion("ggchord")
```

The last line reports your installed version. This local documentation previews
**0.26.0.9000**. The repository's last recorded formal release is **0.16.6**;
new Foundation, Fusion, BEDPE and aligned-character APIs require the matching development checkout. See the
[migration notes](../MIGRATION.md) before updating an existing script.

For development work, install dependencies first and run from the matching
checkout in a fresh R session:

```{r example-2, eval=FALSE}
install.packages(".", repos = NULL, type = "source")
library(ggchord)
stopifnot(as.character(packageVersion("ggchord")) == "0.26.0.9000")
```

Version numbers do not identify individual commits. The downloadable build
manifest records the source revision. This local preview does not imply a
published package or deployed website. Stable users can consult the
[0.16.6 documentation](https://stat.ethz.ch/CRAN/web/packages/ggchord/index.html).

<span id="verified-versions"></span>

#### Source downloads {#installation-source}

Source packages are available from [CRAN](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/ggchord/index.html) and [GitHub v0.16.6](https://github.com/DangJem/ggchord/releases/tag/v0.16.6).

#### Optional dependencies {#installation-support-evidence}

Getting started and the basic chord lessons require only ggchord. The case study lists its extra dependencies.

### Confirm the installation {#installation-troubleshooting}

Load the package in a new R session with `library(ggchord)`. If installation or loading fails, check the R or dependency version named in the error.

## Draw sequence backbones {#chord-start}

Start with four bundled sequences. Read their positions and lengths before adding links and features.

### Draw the backbones {#chord-start-draw}

Run this lesson in a fresh R session after installing the version described on the [installation page](#installation).

```{r example-3, eval=FALSE}
library(ggchord)
```


```{r example-4, eval=FALSE}
p_chord_backbone <- ggchord(seq_data = seq_data_example) +
  geom_seq() +
  geom_seq_label() +
  coord_chord()
view_ggchord(p_chord_backbone, width = 7, height = 7, units = "in")
```


<figure class="documentation-figure"><img src="tutorial-assets/frontbackbone.jpg" alt="Default arc backbones for four sequences" width="1008" height="1008" loading="lazy"><figcaption>Default arc backbones for four sequences</figcaption></figure>

### Read the plot {#chord-start-read}

Each arc represents a row of the sequence table. Find `MT108731.1` by its label and compare it with `MT118296.1`. These two sequences are 64,323 bp and 32,090 bp, so the first arc is about twice as long as the second.

`geom_seq()` draws the backbones, `geom_seq_label()` adds their IDs, and `coord_chord()` arranges the backbones as arcs.

### Try removing the labels {#chord-start-try}

Remove the `geom_seq_label()` line and run the code again. The arcs stay in place and the sequence names disappear.

### Use your own sequences {#chord-start-adapt}

Replace `seq_data_example` with a table containing `accver` and `length`. See [Basic input tables](https://dangjem.github.io/ggchord/en/chord-data.html#tables) for the column definitions. Next, [add links and features](https://dangjem.github.io/ggchord/en/chord-build.html).


## Draw your first collinear plot {#collinear-start}

Start with four bundled sequences in horizontal rows. Use the same input as in the chord chapter and look at the backbones first.

### Draw four backbones {#collinear-start-draw}

Run this lesson in a fresh R session after installing the version described on the [installation page](#installation).

```{r example-5, eval=FALSE}
library(ggchord)
```


```{r example-6, eval=FALSE}
p_linear_base <- ggchord(seq_data = seq_data_example) +
  geom_seq() +
  geom_seq_label() +
  coord_collinear()
view_ggchord(p_linear_base, width = 8, height = 5, units = "in")
```


<figure class="documentation-figure"><img src="tutorial-assets/frontlinearbase.jpg" alt="Four collinear backbones" width="1152" height="720" loading="lazy"><figcaption>Four collinear backbones</figcaption></figure>

### Read position and length on a common scale {#collinear-start-read}

Each row represents one sequence. Compare `MT108731.1` at about 64 kb with `MT118296.1` at about 32 kb. A shared bp scale lets you compare horizontal lengths directly.

### Try removing the sequence names {#collinear-start-try}

Remove `geom_seq_label()`. The four backbones and their relative lengths remain visible.

### Use your own sequences {#collinear-start-adapt}

Supply a sequence table with `accver` and full `length`. Next, [add an alignment and a CDS](https://dangjem.github.io/ggchord/en/collinear-build.html).


## Draw your first circular map {#plasmid-start}

Start with one complete circular backbone using bundled pUC19.

### Draw the backbone and centre label {#plasmid-start-draw}

Run this lesson in a fresh R session after installing the version described on the [installation page](#installation).

```{r example-7, eval=FALSE}
library(ggchord)
```


```{r example-8, eval=FALSE}
plasmid <- plasmid_example_pUC19
p_first_circle <- ggchord(seq_data = plasmid) +
  geom_seq() +
  geom_seq_center_label() +
  coord_circular()
view_ggchord(p_first_circle, width = 6, height = 6, units = "in")
```


<figure class="documentation-figure"><img src="tutorial-assets/firstcircle.jpg" alt="A circular pUC19 backbone with its name and length" width="864" height="864" loading="lazy"><figcaption>A circular pUC19 backbone with its name and length</figcaption></figure>

Ticks extend inward from the inner backbone edge, with labels farther inward. On a narrow canvas, the default removes colliding text while retaining the ticks.

### Read the ticks around the circle {#plasmid-start-features}

One turn represents the full length of pUC19. The origin is at 12 o’clock by default, with coordinates increasing clockwise. Ticks show bp and the centre label identifies the sequence. The backbone and `coord_circular()` establish positions around the circle. The next section places a replication origin on it.

### Use your own sequence {#plasmid-start-adapt}

Provide one sequence row with `accver` and full `length`, and use the same ID in the feature table. [Continue to features and labels](https://dangjem.github.io/ggchord/en/plasmid-build.html).


## HSP Dotplot and radial spokes {#view-expansion}

Use the existing source tables; no extra alignment table is required. Dotplot segments retain all four HSP endpoints. Radial spokes use cyclic existing relationships and proportional lengths. See the website view-expansion chapter for source preparation, supported layers and inverse mapping.

```{r example-9, eval=FALSE}
ggchord(seq_data_example, ribbon_data_example) +
  geom_alignment_segment(aes(link_colour = pident)) +
  coord_dotplot()

ggchord(seq_data_example, ribbon_data_example) +
  geom_seq() +
  geom_link_ribbon() +
  geom_seq_label() +
  coord_radial_synteny()
```
